comments.text:
I left on my own terms at 59- 3 years ago 
Never packaged or laid off after 40 years straight of working - including high school and university 
Never got the”envelope” with the package but trade that off easily for being able to leave on my own terms -that’s priceless to me

comments.text: That's higher than I expected. I am 59 next month and I am OK if i was given a package. I plan on working to 63 but if this happened to me right now, I would just retire and accept a lower but comfortable retirement income

comments.text: Really good information in this video.  I feel there is a lot of guess work involved with planning.  Inflation, health, the list goes on and on.  Scary to think about.  One misstep can really hurt your retirement plan.

comments.text: I started my retirement plan at 25. The goal was 57. At 49 I sat down with my planner and focused on a monthly income number for 57 until death.
comments.author: @ronnyber

comments.text: I would say it did and didn't happen to me.  Back during Covid I was let go.  I was 54 and was planning to work for a couple more years so I could pay off my house.  Once I was let go I sat down and worked out my options and I was thinking I could stop working even with the outstanding amount I still owed on my house.  So I was going going in this direction when two years later an unexpected bill came my way so I ended up taking a contract job to make the money to pay off that bill.  Once the four month contract ended I officially quit working.  By this time I had everything worked out and my debt was under control to the point that I knew when I would have it paid off, which it is now paid off and I have been enjoying life outside work for over two years now.
comments.author: @paulmarshall4794

comments.text: I was lucky. I planned to retire in my early sixties. Shortly after I turned 60, I got an early retirement package.
comments.author: @rickster904

comments.text: I left at 54 with a 60% Defined Benefit pension
comments.author: @DonEByTheREELDeaL

comments.text: Yah we are onto plan F or G now. We went from just planning significant career changes and moving to a new city to shake things up, to a plan to pull pension commuted values and sell the house to do RV full-time/retirement, then couldn't sell the house before the pension transfer age deadline, when finally sold the property covid had hit to prevent planned RV travel, then health issues hit, a medical retirement with family care leave came in, and now hopefully will get an early retirement package... So we could have had a series of five or six vastly different retirement plans at this point....
comments.author: @Regorybles

comments.text: This sort of thing happened to both me and my mother.  My mother was forced into early retirement at age 52 because she acquired a chronic disorder.  I was then forced into early retirement at age 31 due to a car accident and the resulting injury.  Luckily, we had each other as we were able to share the bills and make due.
comments.author: @ryanm7171

comments.text: Great video and I'm a living example of this right now. Soon 59 and my Mag 7 role was recently eliminated. Thankfully I diligently saved for years, stress tested the plan regularly and I may even retire. Modern income generating financial products help greatly.
comments.author: @Income_ETF_Investor

comments.text: This is fantastic advice and I’ve been telling older friends to start their 5 year retirement plan. I was 59 and in year two of my own plan when COVID hit. I took a voluntary package and left my career with 10 days notice. Luckily things have worked out great. It would have been better with more time but I can’t complain since at least I had started to prepare.
comments.author: @djs-YTO

comments.text: great discussion topic
comments.author: @MrZrryan2

comments.text: This exact scenario happened to me.  I was 57 and a planned to work until 60 in a sales role.  Then covid happened and overall sales dropped off, and then my largest customer went bankrupt.  That was the end of my career.  Companies generally don't hire people for sales roles that are pushing 60.   Fortunately, my planner and I sat down and we found out that I could, in fact, quit working and live a good life in retirement.  I  had been working with a financial planner since the 1990's to prepare for just this situation!
comments.author: @robertcarrier3139

comments.text: Sorry to hear, but glad it all worked out!
comments.author: @ParallelWealth

comments.text: Hey Adam- once again a video that makes me double take- first was retire to not from- now - what if you got laid off tomorrow?  questions that relevant but mostly ignored- unless like me- you are scared about retiring with enough money. I have kinda started to look for something to dabble with after i retire but now after seeing the video- um read and learn faster ! I will get ready at a faster pace- just in case. Thanks again for the info and saying out loud what is known but not really paid much attention to ! :)
comments.author: @MM-tw6cm

comments.text:
The thought that you will never get laid off is just so wrong it hurts because being laid off is just one way of losing your job. I had a job that you couldn't get laid off from, but I still lost it due to health reasons. You could also find yourself losing your job because your employer goes out of business, or is taken over and then layoffs become a thing.

Bottom line is you always need to plan, even if you  don't think losing your job is even a possibility.
comments.author: @ColdRunnerGWN

comments.text: I have heard so much talk about "We are living longer so we should work longer" but where I worked I am the only person I know that actually chose their own retirement date (age 61 for me). Even then I was given my severance notice at age 56 but 2 days before my severance date I was able to land a position at another division. Everyone else that I worked with was downsized out of their job in their mid-50s, most never found work again and certainly not at anything like they were making before. If your plan is to work into your mid to late 60s or possibly even your 70s you may find that you employer has other ideas about how long you'll be working there.
comments.author: @ddavidson5

comments.text: My dad took early retirement at 55 as an engineer but then after 3-4 years had to get a job at Walmart as a sales clerk
comments.author: @earthsteward9

comments.text: @earthsteward9  That is unfortunate for your dad. No matter all the "start a second career in retirement" talk in the media I find that it doesn't usually go that way. There are exceptions of course, there's always exceptions, but for most once you hit your mid-50s or older and retire (or are downsized) there's no going back. I would treat the retirement decision as final. If something else comes up that you want to do then great but I wouldn't count on it.
comments.author: @ddavidson5

comments.text: ​ @ddavidson5 Thanks. I am turning 60 this summer and have a high stress job that I can't do until 65. I am training to do data analysis and do that until 70 but I know the odds are against me
comments.author: @earthsteward9

comments.text: I retired at 54. My choice. 60% pension.  Then went on to double dip both part and full time.  Great retirement bonus, plus a severance for my un used sick leave
comments.author: @DonEByTheREELDeaL

comments.text: @DoneBytheOnlyREELDEAL No workplace pension for me but those extra 5 years made the difference between a comfortable retirement or something less than that.  I would have figured out a plan of some kind if it had happened but as it was I made my date, actually I had 60 penciled in but then I took the extra year to be sure. Glad your date worked out for you.
comments.author: @ddavidson5

comments.text: ​ @ddavidson5   I could have stayed to 61 and got a 70% Defined Benefit pension but by leaving early I was freed up to do other jobs. I double dipped for 4 years both part-time and full-time.  I compared it to an old co-worker who will have the 70% pension.  He will start being ahead of me by age 77. After age 70 statistics Canada says you spend 1% less per year. No need for more money when you spend less. I always have my house to sell if I need money.

comments.text: @ColdRunnerGWN  Nope.  68% gone. comments.author: @denislanglois68

comments.text:
@denislanglois68  Even if you made $500K in QC, your average tax rate with CPP and EI would be only 47%, and I'm going to go out on a limb and say that you were well short of that. You're clearly confusing the margin tax rate with the average. The rest, I'm guessing is including a pension deduction, which would reduce your tax rate even more. 

But feel free to post the amounts of an actual pay period that shows you did indeed take home less than 1/3 of your gross pay. I can easily verify the amounts online with the payroll deduction tables.
